lead: A function of two variables is a surface, and this unit gives the toolkit for working with surfaces. You learn to take limits across the plane instead of along a line, differentiate one variable at a time, approximate a surface by a plane, expand it as a Taylor series, and locate its peaks, pits and saddles with and without a constraint.
about: One variable at a time is the whole trick. Chapter 4.1 asks when f(x, y) settles to a single value near a point and gives the two-path test that answers no. 4.2 freezes one variable and differentiates in the other, then repeats for higher orders. 4.3 combines those partials into the total differential and the chain rule, which is what differentiability really means in the plane. 4.4 packs the first partials into a determinant, the Jacobian, with its chain and inverse rules. 4.5 expands f(x, y) about a point in powers of the increments. 4.6 reads the second-degree part of that expansion to sort critical points into maxima, minima and saddles. 4.7 repeats the search on a constraint with Lagrange multipliers, and 4.8 turns partial derivatives into tangent planes and normal lines.

chapters.idea: A limit at a point exists only if f approaches the same value along every path into that point, so two paths with different values kill the limit.
chapters.depth: The ε-δ definition in two variables: for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that 0 < √((x−x₀)² + (y−y₀)²) < δ gives |f(x, y) − L| < ε. Define a neighbourhood as an open disk. State the algebra of limits (sum, product, quotient) and continuity at a point and on a region. Teach the two-path test: find two curves through the point that give different limits, and the limit does not exist; some syllabi call this the path test. Then the polar route: put x = x₀ + r cos θ, y = y₀ + r sin θ and demand a limit as r → 0 that does not depend on θ. Cover continuity of polynomials and of rational functions away from zero denominators, with piecewise examples at the origin. Stop at continuity; uniform continuity and compactness are not needed here.

figure.caption: Along y = x the function xy/(x² + y²) is 0.5 everywhere; along the x-axis it is 0. Two paths, two values, so the limit at the origin does not exist.
figure.aria: Two flat horizontal lines, one at height 0.5 for the path y = x and one at height 0 for the x-axis, over x from 0.1 to 1.

chapters.example: Test f(x, y) = xy/(x² + y²) for (x, y) ≠ (0, 0), with f(0, 0) = 0, at the origin. Along y = mx: f = mx²/(x² + m²x²) = m/(1 + m²), which depends on m. Take m = 1 and get 1/2; take m = 0 and get 0. Two paths, two values, so the limit does not exist and f is not continuous at the origin. In polar form f = (1/2) sin 2θ, which shows the θ-dependence directly.
chapters.trap: Taking the iterated limits — first x → 0 with y fixed, then y → 0 — and calling the answer the limit. Those two may exist and agree while the two-variable limit fails. Also, straight lines y = mx are not all the paths; try y = x² as well.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, for limits, continuity and the algebra of limits of one variable.
chapters.leave: Directional derivatives and the gradient go to Unit 6; continuity of vector fields also goes there.

chapters.idea: A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative taken with every other variable held constant.
chapters.depth: Define ∂f/∂x at (x₀, y₀) as the derivative of the one-variable function x ↦ f(x, y₀), written f_x or ∂f/∂x. Explain the geometry: the slope of the curve cut from the surface by the plane y = y₀. Differentiate with all the one-variable rules, treating the other variable as a constant. Higher orders: f_xx, f_yy and the mixed f_xy, f_yx, by differentiating twice. State the Clairaut/Schwarz theorem — mixed partials agree when they are continuous — and warn that they can disagree otherwise; only a few universities chase an explicit counterexample. Extend to three variables, and to implicit partials from F(x, y, z) = 0: ∂z/∂x = −F_x/F_z.

figure.caption: Holding one variable constant at each step gives the four second partials; the two mixed ones agree whenever they are continuous.
figure.aria: A tree from f splitting into f_x and f_y, each splitting again into two second partials.

chapters.example: For f(x, y) = x³y² + sin(xy), find f_x, f_y and both mixed partials. f_x = 3x²y² + y cos(xy), f_y = 2x³y + x cos(xy). Then f_xy = ∂/∂y(3x²y² + y cos(xy)) = 6x²y + cos(xy) − xy sin(xy), and f_yx = ∂/∂x(2x³y + x cos(xy)) = 6x²y + cos(xy) − xy sin(xy). The two mixed partials agree, as the continuity theorem promises.
chapters.trap: Treating the frozen variable as a constant outside but forgetting it inside a product or a composite: in y cos(xy) the y multiplies the derivative of cos(xy) and also stays as a factor. Also, f_xy = f_yx is a theorem with a continuity hypothesis, not a definition.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for continuity, and Unit 1 for one-variable differentiation rules.
chapters.leave: The total derivative and the chain rule are chapter 4.3; the directional derivative is in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A function is differentiable when a small change in the inputs produces a change that is linear in the increments plus an error that shrinks faster than the distance moved.
chapters.depth: Differentiability, not just partials: f is differentiable at (x₀, y₀) when Δf = f_x Δx + f_y Δy + ε ρ, with ρ = √(Δx² + Δy²) and ε → 0 as ρ → 0. Give the total differential df = f_x dx + f_y dy and read it as the change along the tangent plane. Take the chain rule in three shapes: z = f(x, y) with x = x(t), y = y(t) gives dz/dt = f_x dx/dt + f_y dy/dt; with x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v) give the two-sum forms for ∂z/∂u and ∂z/∂v; and the implicit form dy/dx = −f_x/f_y. Draw the dependency tree for each. Mention Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions, which some syllabi attach to this section. Note that partials may exist while the function is not differentiable, using the example from 4.1.

figure.caption: A change in t reaches z through two routes, one through x and one through y; the two partial rates add.
figure.aria: A downward flow from t to x(t), y(t) to z to dz/dt, with the sum formula written at the last box.

chapters.example: Let z = x²y + y³ with x = t², y = t. Find dz/dt at t = 1. Chain rule: dz/dt = (2xy)(2t) + (x² + 3y²)(1). At t = 1, x = 1 and y = 1, so dz/dt = 2·1·1·2 + (1 + 3) = 4 + 4 = 8. Check by substituting first: z = t⁵ + t³, so dz/dt = 5t⁴ + 3t², which is 5 + 3 = 8 at t = 1.
chapters.trap: Existence of f_x and f_y is not differentiability. The function xy/(x² + y²) has both partials at the origin (both 0) yet is not even continuous there. Also, do not write dz/dx when z reaches x by two different routes.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.2; the one-variable chain rule from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: The directional derivative and the gradient are Unit 6; the tangent plane reading of df is finished in chapter 4.8.

chapters.idea: The Jacobian is the determinant of the matrix of first partials, and it measures how a change of variables stretches area.
chapters.depth: Definition: ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = det [[u_x, u_y], [v_x, v_y]], with rows for the new variables and columns for the old; some syllabi call it the Jacobian determinant. Compute for two and three variables, including a 3×3 example. Properties: the chain rule ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = ∂(u, v)/∂(s, t) × ∂(s, t)/∂(x, y); the inverse rule J · J′ = 1 for a map and its inverse; and J = 0 exactly where the map loses independence, that is, where u and v are functionally related — only a few universities prove this last one. Give the standard Jacobians to remember: r for polar, ρ for cylindrical, ρ² sin φ for spherical. Show where the Jacobian enters a change of variables in a double integral.

figure.title: J = ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)
figure.caption: The Jacobian is the determinant of this 2×2 block: rows for the new variables u and v, columns for the old ones x and y.
figure.aria: A two-by-two array with row u holding u_x and u_y and row v holding v_x and v_y.

chapters.example: For x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, find ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ). x_r = cos θ, x_θ = −r sin θ, y_r = sin θ, y_θ = r cos θ. The determinant is r cos²θ + r sin²θ = r. So a small rectangle in the (r, θ) plane has area r dr dθ in the (x, y) plane, and dx dy = r dr dθ.
chapters.trap: Getting the rows and columns the wrong way round. ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) is not ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v); the two are reciprocals, so the answer r above is not 1/r. Sign slips in the 2×2 determinant are the other common loss.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for partial derivatives and Unit 1 for determinants of small order.
chapters.leave: The actual integration after a change of variables is Unit 5, chapter 5.3.

chapters.idea: A smooth function of two variables can be rebuilt near a point from its partial derivatives at that point, in powers of the two increments.
chapters.depth: Taylor's theorem for two variables: f(a + h, b + k) = f + (h f_x + k f_y) + (1/2!)(h² f_xx + 2hk f_xy + k² f_yy) + …, with every partial evaluated at (a, b). Give the third-degree term too and state the remainder without proof. Maclaurin form is the case a = b = 0. State the condition: continuous partials up to one order beyond the term kept. Point out that the second-degree piece is a quadratic form in (h, k) whose sign is settled in 4.6. Use the expansion for approximations with an error estimate. Only a few universities write the Lagrange form of the remainder for two variables; keep that to one line.

figure.caption: Each degree of the expansion is built from partials evaluated at the base point (a, b), and the remainder is what is left over.
figure.aria: A downward chain from partials at (a, b) to the degree-1 term, the degree-2 term, and then their sum plus a remainder.

chapters.example: Expand f(x, y) = e^x sin y about (0, 0) up to second degree. f(0, 0) = 0. f_x = e^x sin y gives 0, f_y = e^x cos y gives 1. f_xx = e^x sin y gives 0, f_xy = e^x cos y gives 1, f_yy = −e^x sin y gives 0. So f ≈ 0 + (0·h + 1·k) + (1/2)(0·h² + 2·1·hk + 0·k²) = k + hk, that is, f ≈ y + xy.
chapters.trap: The mixed term. Inside the bracket it is 2hk f_xy, and the outside factor is 1/2, so the two cancel and f_xy hk appears with coefficient 1 — students often write 2f_xy hk or ½f_xy hk. Also remember h and k are increments from (a, b), not x and y themselves.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 and 4.3, and Taylor's theorem for one variable from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: The use of the second-degree term in classifying critical points is chapter 4.6.

chapters.idea: At an interior critical point the surface looks like f plus a quadratic form, and the signs of f_xx, f_yy and f_xy decide whether that shape is a bowl, a cap or a saddle.
chapters.depth: Define local maximum and local minimum at an interior point with a disk. Critical point means f_x = f_y = 0, or a partial fails to exist. Second derivative test at a critical point: compute D = f_xx f_yy − f_xy². D > 0 with f_xx > 0 is a local minimum; D > 0 with f_xx < 0 is a local maximum; D < 0 is a saddle point; D = 0 says nothing. Some syllabi call D the Hessian determinant or the discriminant. Give the Taylor reason: the second-degree term in 4.5 decides the sign of f − f(a, b). For absolute extrema on a closed bounded region: interior critical points first, then the boundary as a one-variable problem, then compare values. Include applied word problems such as the open box of largest volume.

figure.caption: The sign of D = f_xx f_yy − f_xy², together with the sign of f_xx, sorts a critical point into a minimum, a maximum or a saddle.
figure.aria: A decision tree from the critical-point equations splitting on D greater than, less than or equal to zero, with the f_xx sign deciding minimum versus maximum.

chapters.example: Find and classify the critical points of f(x, y) = x³ + y³ − 3xy. f_x = 3x² − 3y = 0 gives y = x²; f_y = 3y² − 3x = 0 gives x = y². Substituting gives x = x⁴, so x = 0 or x = 1. Critical points: (0, 0) and (1, 1). Now f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 6y, f_xy = −3, so D = 36xy − 9. At (0, 0), D = −9 < 0: saddle. At (1, 1), D = 27 > 0 and f_xx = 6 > 0: local minimum, value f(1, 1) = 1 + 1 − 3 = −1.
chapters.trap: Using D alone. When D > 0 you must still read the sign of f_xx to separate minimum from maximum. Also, setting f_x = f_y = 0 finds only interior points; the boundary of the region needs its own check.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2, 4.5 and Unit 1 for maxima and minima of one variable.
chapters.leave: Constrained problems are chapter 4.7; definite integrals for volumes are Unit 2.

chapters.idea: On a constraint curve the best point is where the level curve of f just touches the constraint, so the two gradients point along the same line.
chapters.depth: Problem: optimise f(x, y) subject to g(x, y) = c. The method of Lagrange multipliers: solve ∇f = λ ∇g together with g = c, that is f_x = λ g_x, f_y = λ g_y and g = c, three equations in x, y and λ. Some syllabi call it Lagrange's multiplier method. Give the geometric reason: at a constrained optimum the level curve of f is tangent to the constraint curve, so the gradients are parallel. Say what λ measures: the rate at which the optimum value changes as c changes. Check separately any point where ∇g = 0. Compare every candidate and the endpoints of the constraint. Add engineering applications such as maximum volume for a fixed surface area. Two constraints with λ and μ: only a few universities teach it, so one example at most.

figure.caption: The gradient condition and the constraint equation are solved together; the solutions are candidates that must still be compared.
figure.aria: A downward flow from the optimisation problem to the gradient condition and the constraint equation, both feeding into a solve step and a final comparison of candidates.

chapters.example: Maximise f(x, y) = x²y subject to x + y = 3. Here g = x + y, so f_x = 2xy = λ, f_y = x² = λ, and x + y = 3. Equating the two expressions for λ gives 2xy = x², so x(2y − x) = 0. If x = 0 then y = 3 and f = 0. If x = 2y then 3y = 3, so y = 1, x = 2, and f = 4. Comparing, the maximum value is 4 at (2, 1).
chapters.trap: Dividing by x or y before checking whether it can be zero, which silently throws away candidates. Also, the constraint equation is one of the equations to solve — it is not optional, and it is what fixes λ.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.6 for unconstrained extrema, and chapter 4.2 for gradients written out as partials.
chapters.leave: Directional derivatives and ∇f as a vector are treated fully in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The gradient of F at a point of the surface F(x, y, z) = 0 is perpendicular to the surface there, which gives both the tangent plane and the normal line.
chapters.depth: Surface in implicit form F(x, y, z) = 0 and a point P = (x₀, y₀, z₀) on it: the normal vector is ∇F at P, and the tangent plane is F_x(x − x₀) + F_y(y − y₀) + F_z(z − z₀) = 0, all partials at P. For the explicit form z = f(x, y), take F = f(x, y) − z, giving normal (f_x, f_y, −1) at the point. Normal line in symmetric form (x − x₀)/F_x = (y − y₀)/F_y = (z − z₀)/F_z. Read the tangent plane as the linear approximation from 4.3: the total differential is exactly the change along this plane. Angle between two surfaces through the angle between their normals. Leave surface area and surface integrals to Unit 6.

nodes.label: Tangent plane
nodes.note: F_x Δx + F_y Δy + F_z Δz = 0

figure.caption: One gradient does both jobs: the plane through P perpendicular to it is the tangent plane, and the line along it is the normal line.
figure.aria: A downward flow from the surface to its gradient at P, then branching to the tangent plane equation and the normal line ratios.

chapters.example: Find the tangent plane and normal line to z = x² + y² at P = (1, 2, 5). Write F = x² + y² − z, so ∇F = (2x, 2y, −1) and at P this is (2, 4, −1). Tangent plane: 2(x − 1) + 4(y − 2) − 1(z − 5) = 0, that is 2x + 4y − z = 5. Check: at P, 2 + 8 − 5 = 5. Normal line: (x − 1)/2 = (y − 2)/4 = (z − 5)/(−1).
chapters.trap: For z = f(x, y) the normal is (f_x, f_y, −1), not (f_x, f_y, 1); the sign of the z-component is the usual slip. And the partials must be evaluated at P before they go into the equation — leaving x and y in the plane equation is wrong.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for partials and chapter 4.3 for the total differential as the tangent-plane change.
chapters.leave: Surface area, surface integrals, Stokes and the divergence theorem are Unit 6.

links: continuity is the hypothesis behind the mixed-partial theorem
partials are the two coefficients in the total differential
the chain rule in matrix form becomes the Jacobian chain rule
the same example shows a limit can fail while partials exist
the total differential is the tangent-plane change
the partials give the normal vector of a surface
